title: Nature and Diffusion of Gynecologic Cancer-Related Misinformation on Social Media: Analysis of Tweets
screen_reason: Content analysis of 2691 Weibo posts retrieved by breast-cancer and cervical-cancer keywords over 7 randomly chosen weeks. Two medical-school graduate coders classified each medically oriented post as true information or misinformation, and the paper reports the share: 33.87% (524/1547). A share of items judged false against expert medical ground truth, with a stated denominator, so CONTENT.

estimates.date: 7 weeks randomly selected from the 52 weeks June 2015 - May 2016 (abstract says June 2015 to June 2016; data extracted July 2016)
estimates.measure_type: % of medically oriented breast/cervical cancer posts on Weibo coded as misinformation
estimates.denominator: 1547 medically oriented Weibo posts about breast or cervical cancer (of 2691 retrieved; the 1144 posts that 'only expressed personal emotions and experiences that cannot be identified as truth or falsehood' were excluded)
estimates.definition: Two coders categorised each medically oriented post as 1 (=true information) or 2 (=misinformation) within its thematic category (background knowledge, prevention, diagnosis, treatment); misinformation = medically inaccurate content, e.g. 'The HPV vaccine can reduce the risk of cervical cancer by 100%'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation refers to false and inaccurate information that is spread intentionally or unintentionally [14]."
estimates.source_quote: Moreover, 66.13% (1023/1547) of the tweets provided true information and 33.87% (524/1547) contained misinformation. A chi-square test indicated that true information was significantly more prevalent than misinformation, χ21(N=1547)=160.9, P<.001.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Nature of Gynecologic Cancer-Related True Information and Misinformation' (p. 4); Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 2 medical school graduate students with expertise in gynecologic diseases coded all posts after piloting on 280/2691 (10.41%); Krippendorff alpha .95 for thematic category and .91 (background knowledge), .88 (prevention), .93 (diagnosis), .89 (treatment) for veracity. No external fact-check list; veracity judged against the coders' medical expertise.
estimates.moderator_quote: Of the 2691 total tweets on Weibo, 1144 tweets (1144/2691, 42.51%) only expressed personal emotions and experiences that cannot be identified as truth or falsehood. These tweets were excluded from further analysis. The remaining 1547 (1547/2691, 57.49%) tweets contained medically oriented information for which the thematic category and information veracity were coded.
estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated flags an important denominator choice: 42.51% of the retrieved topical posts (1144/2691) were dropped as un-codable before the share was computed, so 33.87% is a share of CODABLE medical posts, not of all cancer-keyword posts. Over the full retrieved corpus the figure would be 524/2691 = 19.5%, which the paper never states, so I did not create that row (R8). Sampling is a keyword corpus over 7 weeks randomly drawn from a 52-week window, so the time series is already collapsed by the authors. Year coded 2015 because the midpoint of the June 2015 - May 2016 window falls in late 2015; the abstract's 'June 2015 to June 2016' and the Methods' 'June 2015 to May 2016' disagree by one month.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Table 1 gives the misinformation share by thematic category, all verbatim: treatment 156/189 (82.5%), background knowledge 287/749 (38.3%), prevention 67/467 (14.4%), diagnosis 14/142 (9.9%). I did NOT create four rows: these are disjoint content strata of the same corpus, not separate countries, platforms, measures or definition variants, and pooling them alongside the main row would double-count the same 1547 posts. An adjudicator who wants topic-stratified rows has the verbatim numbers here — the treatment-vs-prevention contrast is an abstract-level headline. 2) 524/2691 = 19.5% (misinformation as a share of ALL retrieved cancer-keyword posts) is derivable from two verbatim counts but is never stated by the paper; left out, noted on the main row. 3) Diffusion counts (64/524 misinformation posts received any retweet, 72 any comment, 132 any like; 143/1023 true posts retweeted) are engagement denominators for the posts, not shares of misinformation among shares, so no SHARING row: the numerator is 'posts that got any retweet', not 'retweets that were false'. 4) The two most-retweeted false posts received 1143 and 1131 retweets — a bare count, no denominator, so no CONCENTRATION row (fails R1). 5) External figures cited from other studies (Allcott & Gentzkow 1-3 fake news stories; ~one-quarter of adults shared fabricated political news; Gage-Bouchard's one-third of leukemia information inaccurate) belong to other papers and are excluded.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of Weibo. Sampling frame: posts matching two Chinese keyword pairs for breast cancer and cervical cancer, harvested with a Python web crawler for 7 weeks randomly selected from the 52 weeks June 2015 - May 2016 (n=2691); no response rate applies. 1144 emotion/experience-only posts were excluded, leaving 1547 coded for theme and veracity by 2 medical school graduate students with gynecologic expertise after a 280-post pilot. Reliability reported as Krippendorff alpha: .95 (theme), .91/.88/.93/.89 (veracity by theme). Falsehood types derived by conventional content analysis with deviant-case validity check. Limitations acknowledged by authors: single disease domain, data 2 years old at publication.
rob.item6_quote: Second, the 2 coders coded the information veracity of the 1547 tweets. Specifically, the coders categorized each tweet as 1 (=true information) and 2 (=misinformation) for the tweets in the 4 thematic categories.
rob.item10_quote: Moreover, 66.13% (1023/1547) of the tweets provided true information and 33.87% (524/1547) contained misinformation.
